newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says no plans for Zaire military intervention.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says no plans for Zaire military intervention.

text.p: The United States insisted on Monday it has no intention of intervening militarily in Zaire's civil war.

Rebel leader Lawrence Kabila "said over the weekend that the presence of American military forces was a threat to the territorial integrity of Zaire. This is not so. It's simply not so," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He also told a news briefing an airlift to repatriate 20,000 most vulnerable Rwandan refugees, including children and the sick and the elderly, from Zaire was expected to begin later this week.

"The presence of the American military in Gabon, in Congo and on the seas is to be available for any kind of evacuation that should be necessary of American citizens and American government employees," Burns said.
"The United States has no intention -- zero -- of intervening militarily in Zaire to affect the course of the fighting," he said.

Burns reiterated U.S. support for Zaire's territorial integrity and Washington's warning, largely unheeded, that foreign forces from central Africa states like Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda, as well as Angola should stay out of the conflict.

Burns also welcomed Kabila's decision this past weekend to give the U.N. High Commission on Refugees access to the estimated 80,000 Rwandan refugees who are in makeshift camps along the Kisangani-Ubundu railroad, south of the city of Kisangani.

"This is very good news. We welcome Mr. Kabila's cooperation," he said. "This means that UNHCR will be able to transport the most vulnerable of the refugees to Kisangani Airport and airlift them either to Goma or directly to Kigali."
The United States estimates there are 20,000 vulnerable, unaccompanied children, sick and elderly refugees who ought to be airlifted out first.

"The healthier refugees will be transported and repatriated overland by truck. We think the airlift might be able to begin later this week, and we hope that the truck convoy could proceed sooner than that," Burns said.
The United States last week donated $3 million to finance the airlift operation.

Until Saturday, the rebels had insisted the refugees, camped along a rail track south of Kisangani and reported to be dying at the rate of at least 120 a day, had to be repatriated by roads that are virtually impassible.

But intense international pressure on the rebels over the previous two days apparently forced a change of mind on the same day the rebels sat down in South Africa for their first negotiations with Mobutu's crippled regime.
Burns said the situation in Zaire continued to deteriorate and he again called on Kabila and the Zairean government to cease fighting and engage in political talks.
